'''Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment Ltd.''' ('''MLSE''') is a [[professional sports]] and [[commercial real estate]] company based in [[Toronto]], Ontario, Canada. With assets that include franchises in four of the six [[major professional sports leagues in the United States and Canada]], it is the largest sports and entertainment company in Canada, and one of the largest in [[North America]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/nhl/rogers-bell-buy-control-of-mlse-1.997655|title=Rogers, Bell buy control of MLSE|date=December 9, 2011|access-date=April 4, 2020|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation|CBC]]}}</ref>

The company's primary holdings are its major sports franchises, the [[Toronto Maple Leafs]] of the [[National Hockey League]], [[Toronto Raptors]] of the [[National Basketball Association]], [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the [[Canadian Football League]], and [[Toronto FC]] of [[Major League Soccer]], as well as their minor league [[farm team]]s, the [[Toronto Marlies]] of the [[American Hockey League]] (AHL), [[Raptors 905]] of the [[NBA G League]], and [[Toronto FC II]] of [[MLS Next Pro]], respectively. In addition, it owns [[Scotiabank Arena]], home arena of the Maple Leafs and Raptors, and [[OVO Athletic Centre]], practice facility for the Raptors. MLSE also manages or has invested in several other sports facilities including [[BMO Field]], home of Toronto FC and the Toronto Argonauts, [[Coca-Cola Coliseum]], home of the Marlies and future home of the [[Toronto Tempo]] of the [[Women's National Basketball Association]], [[Ford Performance Centre]], practice facility of the Maple Leafs and Marlies, [[BMO Training Ground]] practice facility for Toronto FC and Toronto FC II and home of the [[TFC Academy]], [[Lamport Stadium]], practice facility for the Argonauts, and [[Mississauga Sports and Entertainment Centre]], home and practice facility of Raptors 905.

MLSE was founded by [[Conn Smythe]] in 1931 as a [[public company]] named '''Maple Leaf Gardens Limited''' (MLGL), to act as a [[holding company]] for the Maple Leafs and their planned new arena [[Maple Leaf Gardens]], from which the company got its name. Smythe transferred his ownership of the Leafs to the company in exchange for shares in MLGL, and sold shares in the holding company to the public to help fund construction of the arena. Following the death of majority owner [[Harold Ballard]] in 1990, [[Steve Stavro]] led a controversial bid to buy the company and take it [[Privately held company|private]]. In 2012, the [[Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan]] (OTPP) sold their majority share of the company to a joint venture between [[Rogers Communications]] and [[BCE Inc.]], two of Canada's largest media companies. In 2025, Rogers purchased BCE's 37.5% share of the company for CA$4.7 billion, giving it 75% ownership and valuing the company at {{CAD|12.5}} billion.

While initially primarily a hockey company, with ownership stakes in a number of [[professional ice hockey|minor]] and [[junior hockey]] clubs including the [[Toronto Marlboros]] of the [[Ontario Hockey Association]], the company later branched out to own the [[Hamilton Tiger-Cats]] of the CFL from the late 1970s to late 1980s, before merging with the Raptors, who were constructing the Air Canada Centre at the time, and adopting their current name in 1998. The company launched Toronto FC in 2007, and purchased the Argonauts in January 2018.<ref name=ArgosApprove>{{cite web|url=https://www.argonauts.ca/2018/01/19/mlse-acquisition-toronto-argonauts-approved-cfl-board-governors/ |title=MLSE Acquisition of Toronto Argonauts Approved by CFL Board of Governors |date=January 19, 2018 |access-date=January 19, 2018 |publisher=[[Toronto Argonauts]]}}</ref>

==Corporate history==
{{See also|History of the Toronto Maple Leafs}}

===Founding===
[[File:Maple Leaf Gardens' roof under construction, 1931 (public domain).png|thumb|left|Maple Leaf Gardens roof under construction, pictured in 1931]]
The corporation's roots can be traced back to 1927, when [[Conn Smythe]] organized a group of investors to purchase Toronto's premier hockey franchise, the [[Toronto St. Patricks]] of the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL), which had won [[Stanley Cup]] championships in [[1917–18 NHL season|1918]] (as the [[Toronto Arenas]]) and [[1921–22 NHL season|1922]], from a group headed by [[Charles Querrie]]. The club was playing poorly and minority partner [[Jack Bickell]] contacted Smythe about becoming coach of the team.  However, Smythe told Bickell that he was more interested in buying a stake in the team. Not long after, with the team in trouble financially due to majority owner Querrie having lost a lawsuit to former [[Toronto Blueshirts]] owner [[Eddie Livingstone]] over ownership of the franchise, Querrie put the St. Pats up for sale and agreed in principle to sell them to [[C. C. Pyle]] for $200,000, who planned to move the team to [[Philadelphia]].<ref name=thoughages>{{cite web|url=https://nationalpost.com/sports/nhl/maple-leafs-owners-through-the-ages|title=Maple Leafs' owners through the ages|last=Sandler|first=Jeremy|newspaper=[[National Post]]|date=December 1, 2010|access-date=March 19, 2014|url-status=live|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140320041448/http://sports.nationalpost.com/2010/12/01/maple-leafs-owners-through-the-ages/|archive-date=March 20, 2014}}</ref><ref name=ml1920>{{cite web|title=Maple Leafs History: 1920s |publisher=NHL.com |url=http://mapleleafs.nhl.com/club/page.htm?id=42182|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090816083013/http://mapleleafs.nhl.com/club/page.htm?id=42182|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 16, 2009|access-date=September 14, 2011}}</ref>{{sfn|Shea|Wilson|2016|p=30–31}} After Bickell contacted Smythe to inform him of the sale, Smythe persuaded Querrie that civic pride was more important than money and put together a syndicate that bought the St. Pats. Smythe himself invested $10,000 of his own money and his group contributed $75,000 up front and a further $75,000 due 30 days later, with Bickell retaining his $40,000 share in the team.<ref name=thoughages/><ref name=smythe>{{cite web|url=https://nationalpost.com/sports/hockey/nhl/excerpt-the-lives-of-conn-smythe|title=The Lives of Conn Smythe: From the Battlefield to Maple Leaf Gardens: In 1929 Smythe decided, in the midst of the [[Great Depression]], that the Maple Leafs needed a new arena. [[Arena Gardens]], their then home which they shared with the Marlboros,<ref name=history/> had been built in 1912 and lacked modern amenities.{{sfn|Shea|Wilson|2016|p=45}}  It seated just 8,000, which the Maple Leafs were regularly filling. After considering various locations, the site at the corner of Carlton and Church streets was purchased from [[Eaton's|The T. Eaton Co. Ltd.]] for $350,000,<ref name=smytheyoung/>{{rp|104}} a price said to be $150,000 below market value. A new 12,473 seat (14,550 including standing room) arena, [[Maple Leaf Gardens]] (MLG), was designed by the architectural firm of [[Ross and Macdonald]]. To finance construction, Smythe got backing from [[Sun Life]] for half of the expected $1 million cost.<ref name=smytheyoung/>{{rp|103}} He then formed Maple Leaf Gardens Limited (MLGL) as a management company that would own both the hockey team and the arena.<ref name=smytheyoung/>{{rp|102}} A public offering of shares in MLGL was made at $10 each (${{formatprice|{{Inflation|CA|10|1931}}}} in {{Inflation-year|CA}} dollars),{{inflation-fn|CA}} with a free common share for each five preferred shares purchased.<ref>{{cite news|title=Maple Leaf Gardens, Limited - Prospectus|newspaper=The Globe|date=March 5, 1931}}</ref> Ownership of the hockey team was transferred to MLGL in return for shares. To fund construction of the building, workers were paid 20% of their salary in MLG stock.<ref name=smytheyoung/>{{rp|104–106}}<ref name=bigmoney>{{cite news|title=Big money always part of Gardens story|first=Paul|last=Patton|newspaper=[[The Globe and Mail]] |date=April 13, 1989}}</ref> Construction started on June 1, 1931,<ref name="startwork">{{cite news |title=New Arena Work to Start on Saturday at Midnight|newspaper=[[Toronto Star]]|date=May 30, 1931}}</ref> and MLG was opened five months and two weeks later, on November 12, 1931, at a cost of $1.5 million<ref>{{cite news|url=http://ca.reuters.com/article/domesticNews/idCATRE5B03FL20091201|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201225358/http://ca.reuters.com/article/domesticNews/idCATRE5B03FL20091201|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 1, 2014|title=Toronto's Maple Leaf Gardens gets C$60 million facelift|date=December 1, 2009|access-date=January 26, 2014|work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Maple Leaf Gardens 1931 - Air Canada Centre 1999: History vs. high tech: No design marvel, Air Canada Centre struggles to graft Gardens' history into a high-tech package that bucks the retro trend|date=February 13, 1999|last=Beamish|first=Mike|work=[[Vancouver Sun]]}}</ref> (${{formatprice|{{Inflation|CA|1500000|1931}}}} in {{Inflation-year|CA}} dollars).{{inflation-fn|CA}} The Marlboros also moved to the new arena.<ref name=history/>  Bickell was named the first president of MLG.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hhof.com/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMember.jsp?mem=b197801&type=Builder&page=bio&list=ByName|title=Builders - J. P. Bickell - Biography|publisher=[[Hockey Hall of Fame]]}}</ref>

To help fill dates at the new arena, Smythe acquired an expansion franchise in the professional [[International Lacrosse League]] on behalf of MLGL for the 1932 season,<ref>{{cite news|title=Maple Leaf Gardens granted franchise|date=December 10, 1931|newspaper=The Globe}}</ref><ref name=testolympic/> which was also given the name the [[Toronto Maple Leafs (ILL)|Toronto Maple Leafs]].<ref name=testolympic>{{cite news|title=On The Highways of Sport: Local Seniors Will Test Olympic Team Tonight|date=January 29, 1932|last=Rodden|first=M.J.|newspaper=The Globe}}</ref><ref name=twoteams/> A team named the [[Toronto Tecumsehs (ILL)|Toronto Maple Leafs]] had competed in the first season of the ILL at the Arena Gardens,<ref name=twoteams>{{cite news|title=Two Toronto teams in lacrosse loop|date=January 29, 1932|newspaper=The Globe}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=On the highway of sports: Maroons and Leafs in lacrosse opener tonight|date=June 29, 1931|last=Rodden|first=M.J.|newspaper=The Globe}}</ref> but was renamed the Tecumsehs with the arrival of Smythe's team.<ref name="testolympic"/><ref name=twoteams/> Both teams played at MLG.<ref>{{cite news|title=Maple Leafs score decisive victory|date=June 20, 1932|first=jack|last=Murray|newspaper=The Globe}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=On The Highways of Sport: Tecumsehs' Victory Creates All-Round Tie|date=May 9, 1932|last=Rodden|first=M.J.|newspaper=The Globe}}</ref> Smythe pulled out following the season due to financial losses,<ref>{{cite news|title=On The Highways of Sport: Mustangs on Rampage at U. of T.'s Expense|date=October 31, 1932|last=Rodden|first=M.J.|newspaper=[[The Globe (Toronto newspaper)|The Globe]]}}</ref> and the league did not play the following year.

===Minor hockey expansion===
The company has owned numerous [[minor league]] hockey teams over the years, which have served as developmental [[farm team]]s for the Maple Leafs. A group backed by Smythe and [[Frank Selke]] of the [[Montreal Canadiens]] was awarded an [[American Hockey League]] (AHL) franchise for [[Rochester, New York]] in July 1956, after a local group could not come up with the US$150,000 in capital required by the league.<ref name=eager>{{cite news|last=Marcotte |first=Bob |title=Eager fans embraced arrival of the Rochester Amerks |url=http://www.democratandchronicle.com/article/20110307/NEWS0204/103070318/Eager-fans-embraced-arrival-Rochester-Amerks |newspaper=Democrat and Chronicle |date=March 7, 2011 |agency=Gannett Company |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140221031119/http://www.democratandchronicle.com/article/20110307/NEWS0204/103070318/Eager-fans-embraced-arrival-Rochester-Amerks |archive-date=February 21, 2014 |location=Rochester, New York |pages=1B,4B |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=makesit>{{cite news|title=Rochester makes it - Gains AHL franchise|date=July 3, 1956|newspaper=[[Toronto Daily Star]]}}</ref><ref name=coffers>{{cite news|title=Sale of Rochester hockey team pads Maple Leaf coffers|date=July 7, 1966|newspaper=[[Toronto Daily Star]]|first=Neil|last=MacCarl}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Give Rochester conditional OK on AHL franchise|date=June 20, 1956|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref> The Leafs and Canadiens would each own 27.5% of the team, with the balance sold to Rochester interests.<ref name=eager /><ref>{{cite news|title=Maple Leafs Seek Farm Club in AHL|date=March 18, 1959|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref>  The team was named the [[Rochester Americans]].  The Amerks were a joint affiliate of both the Canadiens and the Maple Leafs,<ref name=makesit/> though the club was operated by the Canadiens.<ref name=control>{{cite news|title=Leafs Purchase Control Of AHL Squad From Habs|date=June 15, 1959|pages=22|work=The Globe and Mail}}</ref> In the summer of 1959 the Maple Leafs bought out the Canadiens' ownership share of the club, giving them a 55% controlling interest, due to concerns that with Montreal operating the club they were giving their prospects priority over those of the Leafs.<ref name=coffers/><ref name=control/>  They purchased most of the remaining 45% in 1963,<ref name=coffers/><ref>{{cite news|title=Rumors Have Pilous Going to Rochester|date=June 5, 1963|pages=15|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref><ref name=19players>{{cite news|title=19 players go: AHL franchise at Rochester sold by Leafs|date=July 7, 1966|last=Rimstead|first=Paul|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref> boosting their ownership share to 98% by November 1964.<ref name=exceeds>{{cite news|title=Nothing Exceeds Like Success|date=November 13, 1964|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref> In July 1966 the Maple Leafs sold the team to a group which included their then General Manager [[Punch Imlach]] for a reported $400,000.<ref name=coffers/><ref name=19players/><ref name=sixtyseven>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gNfXe3VrVHMC&pg=PA31|title='67: The Maple Leafs, Their Sensational Victory, and the End of an Empire|last1=Cox|first1=Damien|author1-link=Damien Cox|last2=Stellick|first2=Gord|author2-link=Gord Stellick|year=2009|publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]]|page=31|isbn=9780470739273}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Saturday sale on shorts|date=July 9, 1966|last=Beddoes|first=Dick|author-link=Dick Beddoes|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Corporate reports: Maple Leaf Gardens notes drop in profit|date=November 7, 1966|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|page=25}}</ref>

==Ownership==

===Conn Smythe===
[[File:Conn smythe.jpg|thumb|Conn Smythe, founder of Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment]]

Although Conn Smythe was the face of MLGL from its founding in 1931, he did not acquire majority ownership of the company until 1947, following a power struggle between directors who supported him as president and those who wanted him replaced with [[Frank J. Selke]]. With the help of a $300,000 loan from Toronto stockbroker and MLGL shareholder Percy Gardiner, and the support of minority partner Jack Bickell, Smythe was able to buy 30,000 shares in MLGL from Gardiner<ref name=powerplay>{{cite news|title=Gardens power plays|date=April 3, 1995|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref> and installed himself as president on November 19, 1947, replacing Edward Bickle.<ref>{{cite news |title=Baseball's bankroll gone |last=Dunnell|first=Milt|author-link=Milt Dunnell|newspaper=Toronto Star|date=July 5, 1965}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Hunter |first=Douglas |year=1997 |title=Champions: The Illustrated History of Hockey's Greatest Dynasties. |location=Chicago, Illinois |publisher=Triumph Books |isbn=1-57243-213-6 |page=50}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Smythe is elected Gardens' president|date=November 20, 1947|newspaper=[[Toronto Daily Star]]}}</ref>  The loan was paid off in 1960.<ref>{{cite book |title=Centre Ice: The Smythe Family, the Gardens, and the Toronto Maple Leafs Hockey Club |last1=Smythe |first1=Thomas Stafford |last2=Shea |first2=Kevin Shea |publisher=Fenn Publishing Co. |year=2000 |location=Bolton, Ontario, Canada |isbn=1-55168-250-8 |pages=156–167}}</ref>  In November 1961, Smythe sold 45,000 of his 50,000 shares to a three-person partnership formed by his son [[Stafford Smythe]], [[Harold Ballard]], and John Bassett (owner of the ''[[Toronto Telegram]]'' and part-owner of the Canadian Football League's Toronto Argonauts) for $2.3 million.  When combined with their own holdings, this gave the Stafford-Ballard-Bassett partnership 87,000 shares, representing 60% of the company.<ref name=thoughages/><ref name=smytheyoung/>{{rp|217}}<ref name=powerplay/><ref name=death>{{cite news|title=Ballard's death laid groundwork|date=December 1, 2010|newspaper=Toronto Star}}</ref><ref name=bassettsells/> Ballard fronted Stafford most of the money for the purchase though a loan he obtained.<ref name=thoughages/><ref name=shakeup>{{cite news|title=Ballard president in shakeup at Gardens|last=Beddoes|first=Dick|author-link=Dick Beddoes|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=October 21, 1971}}</ref>  According to several sources, Conn thought the sale was only to his son,<ref name=thoughages/> and was furious when he learned that Ballard and Bassett were his partners. He had hoped that Stafford would keep MLGL for his son, Tommy.<ref name=smytheyoung/>{{rp|217–218}} However, it is unlikely that Stafford could have raised the millions needed for the deal on his own. Stafford became president of MLGL and governor of the Maple Leafs, with Ballard becoming executive vice president and Bassett chairman of the board.<ref name=powerplay/>

===Harold Ballard, John Bassett, and Stafford Smythe===
In March 1966, Conn sold his remaining MLGL shares and resigned from the board of directors after a [[Muhammad Ali]] boxing match was scheduled for MLG. He found Ali's refusal to serve in the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]] during the [[Vietnam War]] to be offensive,<ref name=smytheyoung/>{{rp|232}} and said that by accepting the fight, MLGL owners had "put cash ahead of class."<ref>{{cite news |title='Cash rated over class' Conn quits |author=McKee, Ken |work=Toronto Star |date=March 8, 1966}}</ref>  Within three years under the new owners, profits had tripled to just under $1 million. Ballard negotiated lucrative deals to place advertising throughout the building, and greatly increased the number of seats in the arena.<ref>''Ballard: A Portrait of Canada's Most Controversial Sports Figure'', William Houston, Summerhill Press, 1984, p. 60.</ref>

Following a [[Royal Canadian Mounted Police]] raid at MLG in 1968, Stafford was charged with income tax evasion, and he and Ballard were accused of illegally taking money from MLGL to pay for home renovations and other personal expenses. Just before the charges were laid, Bassett argued to the board of directors that Stafford and Ballard should be removed from their posts. On June 26, 1969, following an 8–7 vote of the board, Stafford and Ballard were both fired, and Bassett was appointed president of MLGL. However, Bassett did not force Stafford and Ballard to sell their shares, and both men remained on the board.  This proved to be a serious strategic blunder; Stafford was the largest single shareholder in MLGL, and he and Ballard controlled almost half the company's stock between them.  They were thus able to regain control of the board in 1970, and Stafford was once again appointed president.<ref name=powerplay/>  Facing an untenable situation, Bassett sold the 196,200 MLGL shares he controlled to Stafford and Ballard in September 1971 for $5.4 million, which he used to buy out his partners in the Argonauts.<ref name=death/><ref name=bassettsells>{{cite news|title=Bassett sells Gardens stock, buys control of Argos|first=Dick|last=Beddoes|author-link=Dick Beddoes|date=September 2, 1971|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref><ref name=shakeup/> Combined with their 306,295 jointly controlled shares, the transaction gave the Stafford-Ballard partnership 78% of the stock.<ref name=bassettsells/><ref name=shakeup/>  Stafford died in October 1971 of a bleeding ulcer at only 50 years of age, just before his trial was scheduled to begin.<ref name=powerplay/><ref name=death/><ref name=repeats/> Under the terms of Stafford's will, of which Ballard was an [[executor]],<ref name=repeats>{{cite news|title=History repeats itself ... almost|date=March 22, 1999|last=Tedesco|first=Theresa|newspaper=[[National Post]]}}</ref> each partner was allowed to buy the other's shares upon their death. Stafford's brother and son tried to keep the shares within the family,<ref>{{cite news|title=MLG control at stake: Smythe bid for Ballard stock rejected|first=Dick|last=Beddoes|author-link=Dick Beddoes|date=January 5, 1972|newspaper=The Globe and Mail}}</ref> but in February 1972 Ballard bought all 251,545 of Stafford's shares for $7.5 million, valuing the company at $22 million.<ref name=powerplay/><ref name=death/><ref name=rinkrat/><ref name=buyscontrol/><ref name=gardensprez/> Stafford's brother Hugh also sold his shares to Ballard, ending the Smythe family's 45-year involvement in the company. Combined with Ballard's 262,162 shares, this gave him majority ownership of about 70%.<ref name=rinkrat>{{cite news|title=Harrold Ballard: From rink rat to Gardens' boss|date=February 5, 1972|newspaper=Toronto Star|last=Orr|first=Frank}}</ref><ref name=buyscontrol>{{cite news|title=Ballard buys Gardens control for $7,546,350|newspaper=Toronto Star|date=February 4, 1972|first=Milt|last=Dunnell|author-link=Milt Dunnell}}</ref><ref name=gardensprez>{{cite news|title=Gardens' president Harold Ballard to buy Smythe shares|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=February 5, 1972|last=Lutsky|first=Irvin}}</ref>  Six months later, Ballard was convicted of 47 charges, including fraud and theft of money and goods, and sentenced to three years in a federal penitentiary.<ref name=howherold/><ref name=MLH70>{{cite web|url=http://mapleleafs.ice.nhl.com/club/page.htm?id=42187|title=Maple Leafs History - 1970s|publisher=Maple Leafs Sports & Entertainment|access-date=June 27, 2017|archive-date=April 27, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190427013623/http://mapleleafs.ice.nhl.com/club/page.htm?id=42187|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{sfn|Shea|Wilson|2016|p=212}}

===Harold Ballard===
In 1966, Ballard set up a family [[holding company]] named Harold E. Ballard Ltd. (HEBL) for his assets, including his shares in MLGL, as part of an [[estate freeze]].<ref name=assulttrial>{{cite news|title=Son of a Ballard: Assault trial a rehearsal for family fight for fortune|date=September 23, 1989|last=McDonald|first=Archie|newspaper=[[Vancouver Sun]]}}</ref><ref name=follies>{{cite news|title=The Maple Leaf Follies: Who needs hockey? With a team of lawyers fighting for ambitious corporations and the feuding Ballard clan, nothing can compare with the faceoff for Maple Leaf Gardens|newspaper=[[Financial Post]]|date=October 1, 1991|last=Johnson|first=Arthur}}</ref> Ballard distributed 103 [[common shares]] in HEBL, with his three children (Bill, Harold Jr., and Mary Elizabeth) each receiving 34 which were held in [[Trust law|trust]], and his wife Dorothy receiving 1, which Harold would inherit upon her death three years later.<ref name=powerplay/><ref name=assulttrial/><ref name=familyaffair>{{cite news|title=Ballard money a family affair Daughter gets $15.5 million as Harold buys her shares|newspaper=Toronto Star|date=January 25, 1989}}</ref><ref name=missdeadline/> Harold retained 308,000 [[preferred shares]] in HEBL.<ref name=follies/><ref name=faceoffbrewing>{{cite news|title=Faceoff brewing over Ballard's fortune|last=Hurst|first=Lynda|newspaper=[[Montreal Gazette]]|date=February 25, 1990}}</ref>  While the equity of the company was vested in the common stock, both common and preferred shares each received a single vote, ensuring that Harold retained control of the company.<ref name=follies/>

After getting into financial difficulty, Ballard reached an agreement in November 1980 with [[Molson Brewery]] (who at the time owned the Montreal Canadiens) for the company to cover his debt financing charges on a loan of $8.8 million for 10 years in exchange for an option to purchase a 19.9% block of shares in MLGL from HEBL and a right of first refusal on the rest of HEBL's shares.<ref name=powerplay/><ref name=molsonnets/><ref name=molsonpurchase/>  The NHL did not learn of the deal until the late 1980s.<ref name=molsonnets/> In 1982, he offered to sell the company for $50 million, with the arena alone reportedly valued at $11 million, though a stockholders' report the following year placed the value of MLGL at $23.5 million.<ref name=bigmoney/><ref name=price/> When Harold transferred ownership of his personal real estate holdings, which were valued at $2.52 million, to HEBL in January 1989, he acquired 4 newly issued common shares in the company plus a promise of a further $896,472 rather than cash.<ref name=howherold/><ref name=follies/><ref name=faceoffbrewing/> Mary Elizabeth sold her stake in HEBL to her father for $15.5 million in January 1989,<ref name=familyaffair/><ref name=faceoffbrewing/> after originally having a deal to sell the stake to Don Giffin,<ref name=follies/> while Harold Jr. sold his back to HEBL for $21 million in June of the same year.<ref name=powerplay/><ref name=follies/><ref name=missdeadline/><ref name=faceoffbrewing/> Harold secured a loan from Molson for the full amount of his buyout of Mary Elizabeth, using the 34 acquired shares in HEBL as security.<ref name=missdeadline>{{cite news|title=Harold E. Ballard Ltd. misses Molson loan deadline|date=January 3, 1991|newspaper=[[Ottawa Citizen]]}}</ref> Harold Jr.'s shares were subsequently retired.<ref name=faceoffbrewing/> Bill sued his father for $170 million over HEBL's acquisition of Harold Jr.'s stake,<ref name=assulttrial/><ref name=faceoffbrewing/> claiming that he and partner [[Michael Cohl]] had acquired a right of first refusal to purchase the shares for $20 million that February.<ref name=powerplay/><ref name=faceoffbrewing/> Shortly thereafter, HEBL issued Harold 32 common shares and $125,216 in exchange for ownership of his 350,200 personally held MLGL shares and $125,000.<ref name=howherold/><ref name=faceoffbrewing/> Two more new common shares would be granted to Harold to repay the $911,000 debt HEBL owed him from his two transactions with the company.<ref name=howherold/> This gave Harold, who feared that Bill was positioning himself to take over the holding company, control of HEBL.<ref name=powerplay/> Harold did not want his bickering children to inherit MLGL because he feared they would destroy it.<ref name=howherold>{{cite news|title=How Harold Ballard got the Gardens|last=Tyler|first= Tracey|newspaper=Toronto Star|date=November 25, 1990}}</ref>

Though Ballard ran up significant amounts of personal debt during his ownership of MLGL, he made the company very profitable, so much so that MLG became known as the "Cashbox on Carlton Street", referring to the address of the arena.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4tlXuNrwjsYC&pg=PT416|title=The Lives of Conn Smythe|first=Kelly|last=McParland|year=2011|publisher=[[Random House]]|isbn=9780771056864}}</ref> Upon Harold's death on April 11, 1990,<ref name=death/><ref name=repeats/>{{sfn|Shea|Wilson|2016|p=275}} most of his estate, which was worth less than $50 million, was left to charitable organizations.<ref name=deepdebt/> The executors of Harold's will were supermarket tycoon [[Steve Stavro]], Giffin, and [[Donald Crump]]. In November 1990 Molson exercised their option on 19.9% of the company, paying $10,000 for 735,575 of HEBL's MLGL shares, which at the time were valued at $20 million.<ref name=molsonnets/> Due to restrictions against cross-ownership in the NHL, the company set up a trust to hold their stake,<ref name=molsonnets>{{cite news|title=Molson nets share of Maple Leafs|date=November 2, 1990|newspaper=[[Ottawa Citizen]]}}</ref><ref name=molsonpurchase>{{cite news|title=Molson to purchase $20 million in Gardens shares for $10,000|newspaper=[[Kitchener-Waterloo Record]]|date=November 1, 1990}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Molson puts shares of Gardens in trust|first=Tony|last=Van Alphen|newspaper=Toronto Star|date=November 1, 1990}}</ref> and the league instructed them to sell the shares within an "adequate amount of time."<ref name=missdeadline/><ref name=cantpay/><ref name=Molsondeal/> Shortly after the estate, which had limited income due to HEBL still owing name=billjoins/> In early 1991, Molson offered to buy the estate's shares for $40 each.<ref name=billjoins/> In September 1991, Bill sold his HEBL stock to his father's estate for $21 million, giving ===Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan===
In 2003 an agreement was reached to restructure the company with Stavro selling his stake to [[Bell Globemedia]] for a reported $120–150-million after debt repayments,<ref name=longtime/> the other partners converting their debts into equity, and each partner getting a direct ownership stake in the newly renamed MLSE, with MLGH being dissolved.<ref name=isnteverything/><ref name=otppgraphic/><ref name=longtime/> This left Teachers' as the controlling majority owners of MLSE with 58.4%, and minority partners Bell Globemedia (15.4%), TD Capital with (13.5%) and Tanenbaum, who took over as non-executive chairman, with 13%.<ref name=thoughages/><ref name=isnteverything/><ref name=otppgraphic/><ref name=longtime/>  Each owner of MLSE had a right of first refusal on any shares sold, in proportion to their ownership share.<ref name=longtime/><ref name=snapup/>  The same year MLSE was internally valued at over $1 billion by Teachers' in its annual report.  In 2008 the Toronto Star reported that a valuation commissioned by the company concluded that the company was worth US$1.5 billion.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thestar.com/news/gta/2008/01/05/toronto_billionaire_eyes_leafs_empire.html|title=Toronto billionaire eyes Leafs empire|date=January 5, 2008|access-date=January 11, 2014|work=Toronto Star|last=Westhead|first=Rick}}</ref>  On December 5, 2008, CTVglobemedia (the renamed Bell Globemedia) sold half of its 15.4% stake to Tanenbaum for $100 million, making Tanenbaum the second-largest stakeholder with 20.7%.<ref name=otppgraphic/><ref name=longtime/>  The transaction valued the company at $1.2 billion.  On August 20, 2009, Teachers' announced that it had agreed to purchase the remaining 7.7% stake in MLSE owned by CTVglobemedia, bumping their stake to 66%.<ref name=otppgraphic/><ref name=longtime/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thestar.com/business/2009/08/20/teachers_pension_plan_boosting_stake_in_mlse.html|title=Teachers' Pension Plan boosting stake in MLSE|date=August 20, 2009|access-date=April 5, 2014|newspaper=Toronto Star}}</ref>

The acquisition made Rogers the owner of all five of Toronto's teams in the "big six" [[major professional sports leagues in the United States and Canada]].<ref name="empire">{{cite web|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/article/rogers-closes-mlse-deal-now-171752754.html|title=Rogers Closes MLSE Deal, Now Rivals World's Biggest Sports Empires|date=July 2, 2025|accessdate=July 5, 2025|publisher=[[Yahoo Sports]]}}</ref> Its majority ownership of MLSE was consolidated with its existing fully owned sports assets, including the [[Toronto Blue Jays]], [[Rogers Centre]] and [[Sportsnet]], within the [[Rogers Sports & Media]] segment.

Rogers retained an option to purchase the remaining 25% of MLSE owned by Tanenbaum's Kilmer Sports,<ref name="RogersPR2025" /> and on July 6, 2026 Rogers announced that Kilmer had agreed to sell it its equity stake for $4.35 billion, valuing the company at $17.4 billion. Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment Ltd. (MLSE) is a professional sports and commercial real estate company based in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. With assets that include franchises in four of the six major professional sports leagues in the United States and Canada, it is the largest sports and entertainment company in Canada, and one of the largest in North America.
The company's primary holdings are its major sports franchises, the Toronto Maple Leafs of the National Hockey League, Toronto Raptors of the National Basketball Association, Toronto Argonauts of the Canadian Football League, and Toronto FC of Major League Soccer, as well as their minor league farm teams, the Toronto Marlies of the American Hockey League (AHL), Raptors 905 of the NBA G League, and Toronto FC II of MLS Next Pro, respectively. In addition, it owns Scotiabank Arena, home arena of the Maple Leafs and Raptors, and OVO Athletic Centre, practice facility for the Raptors. MLSE also manages or has invested in several other sports facilities including BMO Field, home of Toronto FC and the Toronto Argonauts, Coca-Cola Coliseum, home of the Marlies and future home of the Toronto Tempo of the Women's National Basketball Association, Ford Performance Centre, practice facility of the Maple Leafs and Marlies, BMO Training Ground practice facility for Toronto FC and Toronto FC II and home of the TFC Academy, Lamport Stadium, practice facility for the Argonauts, and Mississauga Sports and Entertainment Centre, home and practice facility of Raptors 905.
MLSE was founded by Conn Smythe in 1931 as a public company named Maple Leaf Gardens Limited (MLGL), to act as a holding company for the Maple Leafs and their planned new arena Maple Leaf Gardens, from which the company got its name. Smythe transferred his ownership of the Leafs to the company in exchange for shares in MLGL, and sold shares in the holding company to the public to help fund construction of the arena. Following the death of majority owner Harold Ballard in 1990, Steve Stavro led a controversial bid to buy the company and take it private. In 2012, the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan (OTPP) sold their majority share of the company to a joint venture between Rogers Communications and BCE Inc., two of Canada's largest media companies. In 2025, Rogers purchased BCE's 37.5% share of the company for CA$4.7 billion, giving it 75% ownership and valuing the company at CA$12.5 billion.
While initially primarily a hockey company, with ownership stakes in a number of minor and junior hockey clubs including the Toronto Marlboros of the Ontario Hockey Association, the company later branched out to own the Hamilton Tiger-Cats of the CFL from the late 1970s to late 1980s, before merging with the Raptors, who were constructing the Air Canada Centre at the time, and adopting their current name in 1998. The company launched Toronto FC in 2007, and purchased the Argonauts in January 2018.
